title: Borrowing from rivals
hookLine: Seneca quotes Epicurus often, taking good ideas from a rival school (Letters 2–29)

cards: A fan of one team sits up late studying the rival team's playbook, admiring it, taking notes. Someone deep in one political camp reads the other side's best writer every week.
It doesn't happen often, and to some people it looks like betrayal. Reading the other side usually means hunting for what's wrong with it.
Seneca, a committed Stoic, did something different, over and over, in his letters to a friend. He kept quoting the founder of the rival school.

teach.h: A GIFT AT THE END OF EACH LETTER.
teach.b: First, the habit. In his early letters to his friend Lucilius, Seneca often ends with a small gift: a saying to take away.
And again and again, the saying comes from Epicurus, head of the Garden, the school Stoics argued against on gods, nature, pleasure and death. Second, how he explains it.

teach.h: NOT A DESERTER, BUT A SCOUT.
teach.b: In Letter 2, Seneca says he likes to cross into the enemy's camp, in Richard Gummere's translation, "not as a deserter, but as a scout." He isn't switching sides. He's going over to bring back what's useful.
The gift from Epicurus that day: contented poverty is an honorable state. Third, his principle. Lucilius seems to have teased him about it.

teach.h: A TRUE THING BELONGS TO EVERYONE.
teach.b: Seneca answers, across several letters, that a true and well-said thing belongs to everyone; the best ideas are public property, whoever said them first. He'll take a good line from anyone. Fourth, what he doesn't do.
He doesn't pretend the schools agree. He keeps his own Stoic views, and later in the letters he argues hard against Epicurean ideas.
Borrowing a good thing isn't the same as giving up your own ground.
And respecting a rival's insight isn't the same as pretending your differences don't matter.
That's harder than either cheering your side or abandoning it: holding your convictions and keeping your ears open, at the same time.

how: Readers of Seneca's letters notice how often he closes with a saying from Epicurus, and many take it as a model for learning from rival views while keeping one's own.

o: a spy sent to find the enemy's weak points
a scout who crosses over to bring back what's useful
a deserter who switches to the rival side for good

he stayed a Stoic, crossing over as a scout, not a deserter.

games.q: you're a Stoic, and the best line you read today came from the founder of the rival school. what do you do?
o: ignore it; it's from the other side.
use it, and say where it came from.
games.why: Seneca passed the line on, credited Epicurus, and stayed a Stoic: a scout, not a deserter.

practice: Bring to mind someone you disagree with, a relative, a writer, a coworker, and let the disagreement be there without resolving it. Then, like a scout, look for one thing they get right: one value, one insight, one fair point.
When you find it, hold it up and look at it, without giving up anything of your own.

wordCard.voice: Explorator. Seneca's word for himself crossing into Epicurus's camp: not a deserter, but a scout bringing back what's useful. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a scout. Seneca crosses into the enemy's camp not as a transfuga, a deserter, but as an explorator.

carryVoice: Your line: borrow the good. A true, well-said thing belongs to everyone. Day six hundred fifty-four, done.
